title: karma: Vivekananda's Karma Yoga lectures · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna…
hook: a father asks his son to break open a seed, and asks what he sees inside
carry: too fine to see, too real to deny
tomorrow: karma: a ghost who needs work, and a dog's curly tail

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhakti road: the gopis, jealous of a bamboo flute, hollow enough to be played. Today, the jnana road, and back to Shvetaketu and his father.

Somewhere near you there's a very big tree. An oak, a maple, or, in India, a banyan, with roots dropping from its branches like ropes, wide enough to shade a whole village meeting. That tree came from a seed smaller than a grain of rice. That part is common knowledge. But what's actually inside the seed? A father in the Upanishads asks his son to look.
screen: `A VERY BIG TREE.` → `FROM A VERY SMALL SEED.` → `LOOK INSIDE.`

segments.voice: We're back in the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, where Uddalaka teaches his son Shvetaketu with things from around the house. Last week, it was salt in water. This time: bring me a fruit from that banyan tree. Here it is, sir. Break it open. It's broken. What do you see? Tiny seeds, sir. Break one of those. It's broken. What do you see there? Nothing at all, sir. And the father says: this finest essence, the one you can't see, from that very thing this great banyan tree stands. Believe it, my dear. Then the refrain: that finest essence is the Self of all this. That is the real. Tat tvam asi. You are that, Shvetaketu. Here's what's clever. When Shvetaketu says nothing, he isn't wrong. He really can't see anything. But the tree is standing right there. The father isn't asking him to stop trusting his eyes; he's showing him their limit. Some things are too fine to see and too real to deny. On the jnana road, knowledge doesn't mean collecting more facts. Shvetaketu already had twelve years of those. It means learning to recognize what can't be pointed at, the way you know the salt by its taste and the seed by the tree. And notice the father's gentleness: my dear, believe it. Knowledge here begins with trust, and then becomes seeing.
screen: `BREAK THE FRUIT. BREAK THE SEED.` · `NOTHING AT ALL, SIR.` · `FROM THAT, THE GREAT TREE STANDS.` · `TOO FINE TO SEE, TOO REAL TO DENY.` · then, large: `TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Imagine a single seed in your palm, so small you could lose it, then picture the whole tree that could come from it: trunk, branches, a thousand leaves moving in the wind. Turn the picture gently toward yourself and ask what's the finest thing in you, too fine to see; don't try to find it, just rest with the question, the way Shvetaketu stared at the broken seed. If you pray, you can offer the question.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. On the jnana road today, the action is small: break the seed, look, and trust what you can't see.
Your line: too fine to see, too real to deny. Nothing at all, and a whole banyan. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 310 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA — THE GHOST AND THE CURLY TAIL.`

howItsDone: The banyan seed teaching of the Chandogya Upanishad is taught in Vedanta classes, sometimes with an actual fruit broken open, and the banyan tree itself is honored in many Hindu villages and temples.

chat.says: When Shvetaketu found nothing inside the seed, was he wrong?
options: No. He couldn't see it, yet the whole tree stands from that fine essence.
Yes. He broke it carelessly and missed the tiny tree hiding inside.
No, and his father agreed the tree came only from soil and rain.
chat.meaning: Shvetaketu really saw nothing, yet from that unseen essence the banyan stands. That finest essence is the Self: tat tvam asi.
